title: Cohabitation caused by a man deceitfully inducing a belief of lawful marriage
note: IPC 493 and BNS 81 require a man’s deceit, a woman not lawfully married to him, belief that she is lawfully married to him, and cohabitation or sexual intercourse caused by that belief. Explain the causal chain from deceit to belief to conduct. A promise to marry in the future differs from a representation that a lawful marriage already exists. Both provisions provide imprisonment of either description up to ten years and liability to fine.
statutoryText: Every man who by deceit causes any woman who is not lawfully married to him to believe that she is lawfully married to him and to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him in that belief, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
statusNote: Historical IPC text supplied for study; identify the conduct date and apply the corresponding BNS provision where applicable.

title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife
note: The accused must have a living husband or wife and contract a further marriage that is void because it occurs during that spouse's lifetime. Establish the first marriage, its subsistence and the subsequent marriage under the applicable marriage law. Cohabitation or a bare allegation of marriage does not replace the required proof. Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to seven years and liability to fine. The exception covers a former marriage declared void by a competent court, or a spouse continuously absent for seven years and not heard of as alive during that time, provided the known real facts are disclosed to the new spouse before the subsequent marriage. Mere separation or a pending divorce petition is not itself a dissolution.
statutoryText:
Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Exception.—This section does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction,

nor to any person who contracts a marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years, and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time provided the person contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her knowledge.
statusNote: Historical IPC text supplied for study; identify the conduct date and apply the corresponding BNS provision where applicable.

title: Same offence with concealment of former marriage from person with whom subsequent marriage is contracted
note: IPC 495 depends on the offence in IPC 494: first establish bigamy, then prove concealment of the former marriage from the person entering the subsequent marriage. BNS 82(2) consolidates this aggravated offence. The maximum is ten years’ imprisonment of either description, with liability to fine. Disclosure avoids the concealment element but does not by itself validate an otherwise prohibited second marriage or remove the underlying bigamy offence.
statutoryText: Whoever commits the offence defined in the last preceding section having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
statusNote: Historical IPC text supplied for study; identify the conduct date and apply the corresponding BNS provision where applicable.

title: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage
note: IPC 496 and BNS 83 focus on going through a marriage ceremony dishonestly or with fraudulent intention, knowing that lawful marriage does not result. Prove both the ceremony and the specified knowledge and mental element. A ceremony that is invalid through an honest mistake is not automatically criminal under this provision. Unlike IPC 493, induced cohabitation or intercourse is not a stated ingredient. The maximum is seven years’ imprisonment of either description and liability to fine.
statutoryText: Whoever, dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, goes through the ceremony of being married, knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
statusNote: Historical IPC text supplied for study; identify the conduct date and apply the corresponding BNS provision where applicable.

bns: No BNS counterpart - unconstitutional IPC provision
title: Adultery
note: The Supreme Court in Joseph Shine v. Union of India, decided on 27 September 2018, struck down IPC 497 as unconstitutional. The judgment also invalidated the related CrPC 198 rule to the extent it concerned prosecution for adultery. Do not present the former IPC penalty as an enforceable criminal punishment. BNS contains no corresponding adultery offence. Adultery may still have matrimonial consequences under the applicable law; decriminalisation does not decide every civil or service-law question. It does not remove the ingredients of separate offences involving deceit, coercion or bigamy.
statutoryText: Whoever has sexual intercourse with a person who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of another man, without the consent or connivance of that man, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, is guilty of the offence of adultery, and shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both. In such case the wife shall not be punishable as an abettor.
statusNote: Historical text only — IPC 497 was struck down as unconstitutional in Joseph Shine v. Union of India on 27 September 2018. Its former punishment is not enforceable; there is no BNS adultery counterpart.

title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman
note: BNS 84 covers taking or enticing away a woman known or reasonably believed to be another man's wife with intent that she have illicit intercourse with any person, and concealing or detaining such a woman with that intent. Prove the relevant act, marital-status knowledge or reason to believe, and specified intent. Unlike IPC 498, the BNS text does not retain the express words requiring taking or enticing from the husband or a person having care of her on his behalf. Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to two years, or fine, or both. This is not a replacement adultery offence: suspicion of a relationship does not alone prove every element. Assess the woman's autonomy and the actual conduct without treating her as property.
statutoryText: Whoever takes or entices away any woman who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of any other man, from that man, or from any person having the care of her on behalf of that man, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or conceals or detains with that intent any such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
statusNote: Historical IPC text supplied for study; identify the conduct date and apply the corresponding BNS provision where applicable.
